qrdBas-a14289-d1e101.summary: Rubric for the sixth prologue question of Book 1.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e108.summary: States the question in four members: whether the habit of theology is one undivided habit, distinct from all naturally acquirable sciences, subalternating any of them to itself, or subalternate to any.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e126.summary: First argument that theology is one habit: what is first and noblest in each genus is most one (Metaphysics X), and theology is the first and noblest science or scientific habit.
claims: The first and noblest in a genus is most unified.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e139.summary: Second, that theology is not distinct from other sciences, especially metaphysics: Metaphysics XII has the same subject under the same ratio, God, not God as being, since the attributes investigated there (pure act, life, intelligence, one prince) belong to God alone. And the theologian has no other knowledge of his terms than the metaphysician, so no other habit, if science is just a heap of species in the intellect.
claims: Metaphysics XII treats God under the same ratio as theology.
Theologian and metaphysician share the same knowledge of terms.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e175.summary: Third, that theology is subalternate to metaphysics: its subject, God, falls under being, metaphysics' subject; and it takes as principles things proved in metaphysics and physics, that God is highest being, pure act, and first mover.
claims: Theology's subject falls under metaphysics' subject.
Theology takes principles proved in metaphysics and physics.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e191.summary: Fourth, that theology subalternates all others: it gives the propter quid of all their principles through its subject, which virtually contains the other subjects; and it prescribes the end to all and directs them, as architectonic arts do (navigation over shipbuilding, military over bridle-making).
claims: Theology gives the reasoned fact of all sciences' principles.
Theology prescribes ends to all sciences as architectonic.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e209.summary: Against: theology is not one, since it considers what belongs to different powers, the eternal (scientific part) and the doable (calculative part) (Ethics VI). It is distinct from others, resting on the light of faith rather than natural light. It subalternates none, since all others are evident and it is not. It is subalternate to none, since none can make its principles evident.
claims: Theology spans speculative and practical objects.
Theology rests on the light of faith, distinct from natural light.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e238.summary: First step: set out opinions on the members of the question.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e245.summary: Second step: show how a science can be called one and distinct from others.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e256.summary: Fourth step: respond to arguments against the author's view. The last words begin the first opinion.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e263.summary: First opinion on the first member: theology is simply one undivided habit, and so distinct from any other.
claims: Theology is simply one undivided habit.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e274.summary: First reason: a science is one that is of one subject under one first formal ratio (Posterior Analytics I); theology is such, as shown earlier.
claims: Unity of subject under one ratio makes a science one.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e285.summary: Second reason: the multiplicity of objects does not prevent unity, since there is one primary object, from which alone a science takes unity, not from matter or secondary objects; and a habit lacking evidence from its object is not distinguished by its objects, else faith would be as many habits as there are credibles, contrary to Ephesians 4 ('one faith').
claims: A science takes its unity from its primary object, not secondary objects.
Non-evident habits like faith are not multiplied by objects.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e311.summary: Third reason: in essentially ordered things there must be a stop at something one; cognitive habits are essentially ordered with no infinite regress, so there is a first, which can only be theology, since any other would be nobler.
claims: Essentially ordered cognitive habits reduce to one first habit, theology.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e338.summary: Fourth reason: theology arises more immediately from divine wisdom and knowledge, which is supremely one. The paragraph's last words introduce the contrary opinion.
claims: Theology derives from the supremely one divine wisdom.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e345.summary: Contrary opinion: theology is not simply one habit but simply several, though in a way more one than other sciences like geometry and arithmetic compared together.
claims: Theology is simply several habits, though more unified than unrelated sciences.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e358.summary: First proof: a habit is not simply one if it has several objects simply and first, not by attribution of one to another. Theology has an eternal, purely speculable object and a doable, purely practicable good, treated distinctly. Theologians must treat virtue as much as philosophers do, and theology treats action not for speculation but so that we become good, far more than the Ethics, with a nobler end. Since moral matters have a distinct science among philosophers (Ethics), the theologian too has distinct moral and speculative sciences.
claims: Theology has distinct speculative and practical objects, not related by attribution.
Theological moral science is distinct from speculative theology, as ethics from physics.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e415.summary: Second proof: beings agree in being no less than in relation to God, yet because of their agreement in being there is not one science of all beings (metaphysics, ethics, physics are distinct); so neither does attribution to God make one theology of all things.
claims: Common attribution to God no more unifies sciences than common being.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e441.summary: Third proof: metaphysics treats God as end, in whose contemplation Aristotle placed happiness and the end of virtues (Ethics X), yet does not treat virtues; so theology's treating actions as ordered to God as end does not make it one habit with theology of eternal things. Then (second point) they say theology is one by unity of light, of aggregation in Scripture, and of order to one end, beatitude.
claims: Ordering actions to God as end does not unify moral and speculative theology.
Theology is one by light, aggregation in Scripture, and order to beatitude.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e467.summary: But these do not give simple unity, since, as others argue, the first would make all natural sciences one science, which is false.
claims: Unity of light does not give simple unity, or all natural sciences would be one.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e492.summary: Further: diversity of light does not simply diversify a science, as the same vision occurs in sunlight or candlelight; light does not make the object same or different but manifests it, and so too the habit. Nor does aggregation in one volume, nor order to one end, since all sciences are ordered mediately or immediately to beatitude.
claims: Light manifests but does not constitute identity of object or habit.
Aggregation and common end do not unify sciences.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e521.summary: Second member: it is said that theology is distinct from all others.
claims: Theology is distinct from all other sciences.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e528.summary: One reason: a science with a subject distinct from all others under a distinct ratio is distinct; theology has God under the ratio of deity as total, adequate, first formal subject, which no naturally acquirable science has. Against Metaphysics XII, they say God is considered differently there, or Book XII is not a separate science but part of metaphysics, whose subject is being.
claims: Theology's subject under its ratio is unique among sciences.
Metaphysics XII is a part of metaphysics, whose subject is being.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e554.summary: Others: sciences with different principles are distinct; theology's principles, the articles of faith, differ from others'.
claims: Theology is distinct by its principles, the articles.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e565.summary: Third reason: evident sciences differ from the non-evident; natural sciences are evident from pure nature, theology not.
claims: Theology's inevidence distinguishes it from natural sciences.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e574.summary: Others: a science had only presupposing faith differs from those that can be had without faith by unbelievers. The paragraph closes by introducing the third member.
claims: Theology presupposes faith; other sciences do not.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e588.summary: Third member: some say theology subalternates all others, since the science giving the propter quid of all others' principles subalternates them (as geometry does optics); others resolve their principles to fallible sensory experience and know them only quia, while theology resolves them to their propter quid cause, God.
claims: Theology resolves other sciences' principles to their first cause, God.
Other sciences know their principles only quia, by experience.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e614.summary: Regarding practical sciences, theology subalternates them by prescribing their due end and ordering them to it, as the architectonic art subalternates the manual.
claims: Theology subalternates practical sciences by prescribing their end.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e627.summary: Hence they conclude on the fourth member that theology is subalternate to none, since there is no circle in subalternation.
claims: Theology is subalternate to no other science.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e638.summary: Others hold the contrary: theology subalternates none. It does not give the propter quid of other sciences' principles, since each resolves its principles to the per se ratio of its own subject, which contains the predicate whether or not it comes from God; even if, per impossibile, the triangle were not from God, its ratio would contain having three angles equal to two right angles, as necessarily as triangle is triangle. That man is man has no cause, though there is a cause of man existing.
claims: Each science resolves its principles to the ratio of its own subject.
Essential truths hold independently of their cause of existence.
Theology does not give the propter quid of other sciences' principles.
concepts: cause of being versus cause of essence

qrdBas-a14289-d1e677.summary: Further: an evident science cannot be subalternate to a non-evident one (though, for some, a non-evident science can be subalternate to a non-evident one, as theology to the blessed's science), since the subalternate cannot have greater evidence than the subalternating; theology is not evident, so it does not subalternate the evident natural sciences.
claims: An evident science cannot be subalternate to a non-evident one.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e699.summary: Fourth member: some say theology is subalternate to no human science, for the reason given in the third member, that it subalternates them all.
claims: Theology is subalternate to no human science.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e709.summary: Others give another reason: if theology were subalternate to any science it would be metaphysics, but though God falls under being, he adds nothing outside the ratio of being, unlike the visual line, which adds to the line absolutely.
claims: God adds nothing outside the ratio of being, so theology is not subalternate to metaphysics.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e725.summary: Others: theology does not take its principles from metaphysics, so is not subalternate to it, since its principles are the articles, and its conclusions about God (that God is triune) cannot be proved from being or from anything proved in metaphysics. Ends the first article. Second article: how a science is called one. 'Science' virtually is the simple understanding of a subject virtually containing demonstrable properties, not properly science, since by that measure understanding of principles would be science too.
claims: Theology does not take principles from metaphysics.
Science virtually taken is simple understanding of a subject, not science properly.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e773.summary: Science formally is the habit of a demonstrated conclusion, propter quid or quia, extended to any conclusion deduced from certain premises, evident or believed, in which sense theology is science. As virtual science concerns a simple object, formal science concerns first a complex concluded object, the conclusion, as understanding concerns principles.
claims: Formal science is the habit of a demonstrated conclusion.
The primary object of formal science is a conclusion, a complex.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e806.summary: Hence, as acts of simple understanding of simply diverse objects are distinct (since there is no greater diversity in the prior than the posterior), so habits understanding distinct principles are distinct, and so are scientific habits about distinct questions, wherever understanding and science are really distinct from simple intelligence.
claims: Distinct conclusions have distinct scientific habits.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e837.summary: So the opinion is false that all complexes reducible to one simple incomplex first object make one formal science, a single simple habit, one in most specific species.
claims: Conclusions reducible to one subject do not form one specifically simple habit.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e853.summary: Their proofs: Aristotle (Posterior Analytics I) says one science is of one genus of subject; and as object to power, so subject to science, a power being one by one first incomplex object. But the first object of formal theology is not the incomplex subject but a complex deduced conclusion, belonging to the third act of the intellect. Several conclusions, ordered or not, are distinct habits essentially, since one can be had without another (prior without posterior, or independent questions), and nothing can be had without what is essentially the same as itself.
claims: The first object of formal science is a complex conclusion, not an incomplex subject.
Habits of different conclusions are essentially distinct, since separable.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e915.summary: Reply to Aristotle: he takes science not strictly formally but together with simple understanding of the subject, and for all formal sciences reducible to that simple object, as geometry is called one science as an ordered whole of simple understanding, many understandings of principles, and as many specifically distinct sciences as conclusions, constituting one total science by order of reduction to principles and subject. There is unity of order and of proximate genus, not of most specific species.
claims: Geometry is one science only as an ordered whole of many specific habits.
A total science has unity of order, not specific unity.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e965.summary: Reply to the power-object argument: if valid, all habits of one power would be one habit with one first incomplex object, as the power is.
claims: The power-object analogy would make all habits of one power one habit.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e985.summary: Power and habit are not alike (as said in q2): a power, being less limited and extending to many things, remains one however its acts and habits vary, and so can have one object; not so acts and habits.
claims: A power stays one across varied acts; acts and habits do not.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e1005.summary: Further: the first object of one scientific habit is necessarily one, namely one deduced conclusion, as unity of object is required for unity of lower, more restricted powers; whether higher powers like intellect and will have one first object in creatures the author neither asserts nor denies. The paragraph ends by beginning the next point.
claims: The first object of one scientific habit is one conclusion.
It is uncertain whether intellect and will have a single first object.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e1027.summary: So unity of conclusion is necessarily required for the unity of our science, and hence unity of subject, since a proposition cannot be formed from a subject not one.
claims: Unity of a science requires unity of conclusion and subject.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e1038.summary: Second, unity of subject or conclusion is necessary but not sufficient; unity of middle or principle is also required. The physicist and the astronomer prove the earth's roundness through different middles (equal tendency of heavy parts to the centre; rising and setting of stars).
claims: Unity of the middle term is also required for a science's unity.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e1063.summary: Further: the same conclusion can be demonstrated propter quid and quia, which are not the same science, so unity of conclusion does not suffice.
claims: Propter quid and quia demonstrations of the same conclusion are different sciences.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e1074.summary: Further: the same conclusion can be demonstrated through different causes alone (final, efficient, formal), giving different demonstrations and sciences.
claims: Demonstrations through different causes yield different sciences.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e1087.summary: Further: faith and vision are of the same object but not the same knowledge, vision being immediate and faith mediated by authority; so knowledges through different middles are of different kinds. Aristotle (Metaphysics VI) distinguishes physics and metaphysics by different definitions of the same (snub versus aquiline). Yet perfect propter quid science, whose middle is the complete definition including all causes, cannot vary by middle, since there is only one complete definition. Imperfect propter quid science (through one cause), or quia science, can vary by middle with the same subject and conclusion. So specific unity requires unity of conclusion, subject, and middle. Among abstractive sciences of the same object through the same perfect middle there is no specific plurality, though intuitive and abstractive can differ.
claims: Specific unity of science requires unity of conclusion, subject, and middle.
Perfect propter quid science through a complete definition admits only one middle.
Imperfect or quia sciences can vary by middle.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e1165.summary: Third, some say unity of light is also required, though never sufficient without the rest: with diverse lights, even with the same conclusion and middle, there is not the same science, as the blessed's and a wayfarer's knowledge that a triangle has three angles equal to two right angles differ in kind, since the wayfarer's could never equal the comprehensor's however intensified.
claims: Some hold that unity of light is required for a science's unity.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e1194.summary: Further for that view: effects are diversified by their per se causes; light is a per se cause of scientific act and habit, as the agent intellect's light is (De anima III), so diverse light diversifies scientific act and habit.
claims: Light, as per se cause of knowledge, diversifies it.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e1218.summary: Counter-argument to the light view, drawn from others' positions: light is not a per se cause of scientific habit or act in any genus. Not as material cause or subject, which is the possible intellect, nor as a disposition of the subject, since the possible intellect is immediately disposed to receive every act and habit; hence some deny an impressed species prior to the act, the power being immediately ordered to the act.
claims: Light is not the material cause or disposing condition of scientific habit.
The possible intellect is immediately disposed to its acts.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e1250.summary: Further: the intellect is as immediately disposed to habit or act as to the light, which is itself a habit or act. Light is not an efficient cause: on their view it is one in subject with the possible intellect and cannot move it, and the agent intellect, the natural light, acts on phantasms only privatively, removing impediments. Bodily light disposes the medium, not object or sight. Nor is light a final cause (it is prior to the habit, whose end is the object or act), a formal cause, or matter. So habits are not diversified by lights, and unity of light is not required.
claims: Light is not an efficient, final, formal, or material cause of scientific habit.
The agent intellect acts on phantasms only by removing impediments.
Diversity of lights does not diversify habits.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e1326.summary: Further: a habit does not get its unity from what only manifests its object or unity, since manifesting presupposes unity, and light is only manifestative ('in which' or 'under which'). Which view is truer the author leaves in doubt. The paragraph's last words introduce another proposed requirement.
claims: Light manifests but does not cause unity or distinction of habits.
Whether unity of light is required is left undecided.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e1348.summary: Fourth, some say specific unity of scientific habit or act requires specific unity of its immediate subject, since diversity of matter suffices to diversify effects. The author rejects this: specific unity of subject is no more required for cognitive habits than for appetitive ones, where it plainly is not. Charity and beatitude are of the same kind in angel and man, else human charity could never equal an angel's.
claims: Specific unity of the receiving subject is not required for specific unity of a habit.
Charity and beatitude are the same in kind in men and angels.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e1381.summary: The principle that diversity of matter diversifies effects is not universally true, especially for accidents following the whole composite: quantity of the same kind is received in man and ass. It holds only when subject and accident determine each other adequately, as substantial forms determine their matter. Intellectual habits and acts do not regard the specific ratio of their subject, else man could never have as noble a habit as an angel (false of Christ's soul), but the generic intellectual nature common to all.
claims: Accidents can be of the same kind in specifically different subjects.
Intellectual habits regard the generic intellectual nature, not the specific nature of the subject.
Christ's soul has habits as noble as an angel's.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e1436.summary: Conclusion: specific unity of the subject is not required, but unity of first object or subject and of middle is necessary; light is left in doubt. Divine science is really one: it is the same as the essence, the first object; it is infinite in its ratio; it is adequate to the first object; and it is simply first. Ends the second article.
claims: Specific unity of science requires unity of first object and middle.
Divine science is really one, being identical with the divine essence.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e1467.summary: Third article: answering the question about theology, beginning with its unity, first of God's theology, then the blessed's, then wayfarers'.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e1479.summary: God's theology is simply one habit, really infinite, and its act, God's understanding, is one adequate act by which he knows all at once most perfectly. Succession or plurality of acts and habits in a power is an imperfection; where the act is infinite and regards an infinite first object virtually containing all things and totally comprehended, a plurality of really distinct acts or habits is unnecessary, indeed impossible, since one is adequate to all. An objection is raised: they differ formally from the nature of things.
claims: God's theology is one infinite habit and act.
Plurality of acts in a power is an imperfection.
A single infinite act is adequate to all objects.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e1516.summary: Reply: there can be a formal distinction in God among absolutes only for those whose quidditative rationes signify pure perfections. Understanding absolutely is a pure perfection, but 'this or that understanding', specifically distinguished, implies limitation and imperfection, so it cannot be distinguished in God formally or really. God has one formally infinite understanding, adequate to his intellect and really identical with it and its object; likewise one theology and one infinite habit. By our mode of understanding, this one act is distinguished according to its objects: as bearing on simple terms (above all God under deity) it is simple understanding; on complex principles, understanding of principles, diversified by reason according to them; on demonstrated conclusions of necessary theology, science properly, multiplied by reason according to the conclusions.
claims: A formal distinction of absolutes in God holds only among pure perfections.
Specific kinds of understanding imply limitation and are not formally distinct in God.
God's one act is distinguished only by our reason into simple understanding, understanding of principles, and science.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e1597.summary: Likewise for God's theology of contingents, according to the distinct contingent complexes deduced. God knows all by one simple act and habit really, by infinite actuality, yet by our mode of understanding, arising from experience, acts and habits are distinguished in him with an order of reason like the real order where they are really distinct, as in us: the act bearing on a simple term is prior by reason to itself bearing on a principle, and so on through conclusions in their order.
claims: God's single act has an order of reason mirroring the real order of distinct acts in us.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e1649.summary: On the distinctness of God's theology: since God's theology is all his knowledge without imperfection, most perfect science of every knowable through deity, no other science can be posited in him, taking theology as a whole like geometry, but with only rational, not real, distinction of its acts. It is distinguished from every other science or cognitive act as the intrinsically divine from anything extrinsic and non-divine.
claims: God's theology is all his knowledge, and no other science exists in him.
It is distinct from every other science as divine from non-divine.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e1695.summary: On subalternation, God's theology neither subalternates any science nor is subalternate to any. It is subalternate to none, being simply first among sciences as God among beings, and noblest and most certain, which conflicts with every condition of a subalternate science.
claims: God's theology is subalternate to no science.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e1715.summary: That it subalternates none is harder to see, since its primacy suggests it subalternates all. But subalternating and subalternate sciences can be had by the same intellect: one with a subalternate science, knowing its principles only quia, can know them propter quid through the subalternating one. God's theology cannot be had in the same intellect with other formal sciences.
claims: Subalternating and subalternate sciences must be co-possessable in one intellect.
God's theology cannot coexist with other sciences in one intellect.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e1742.summary: Further: one with the subalternating science can have the subalternate; no one with this can have any other. Objection: it subalternates others because their principles resolve to it, since the line is known more perfectly through the divine essence, as God knows it, than through its own ratio in geometry; and it prescribes their end as most architectonic, master of all.
claims: Objection: other sciences' principles are known more perfectly through God's theology.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e1779.summary: Reply: though principles, objects, terms, and conclusions of other sciences are known more clearly and perfectly through God's theology, other sciences have from themselves, or from what they are subalternate to, the means to know their principles and conclusions certainly and scientifically. The exception is our theology, which is not science and has evidence neither from itself nor from the blessed's science. Further, one with another science can never declare its principles through God's science, which he cannot have. And if clearer knowledge of the same sufficed for subalternation, one person's geometry would be subalternate to another's clearer geometry.
claims: Other sciences have their own sufficient sources of evidence.
Greater clarity of knowledge does not constitute subalternation.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e1831.summary: Reply to the second: God's science is mistress of all but does not properly subalternate them though superior, more certain, and prescribing their end, any more than metaphysics, nobler than all, free and for its own sake (Metaphysics I), subalternates them. So God's theology neither subalternates nor is subalternated. Then begins the blessed's theology.
claims: Being superior and prescribing ends does not constitute subalternation.
Metaphysics, though highest, does not subalternate the other sciences.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e1860.summary: On the unity of the blessed's theology: the act of simple understanding of the divine essence and of all simples through it, as ratio cognoscendi and first known object, is one and the same beatific act in substance, as Augustine says tentatively (De trinitate XV: 'perhaps... we shall see our whole knowledge in one glance'). Yet it is varied and multiplied by reason according to its objects, no less than God's act. The same holds for morning knowledge of the Word and of simple terms in the Word.
claims: The beatific act is one in substance though distinguished by reason according to its objects.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e1897.summary: The divine essence, known intuitively or abstractively with evidence, is the ratio of understanding all quiddities of terms and their necessary complexes. So the blessed's act knowing God and all terms and necessary complexes is one simple act, really undivided but distinguished by reason, as with God's science. Their theology is one act with God, an infinite object, as first object. Understanding of principles and conclusions need not be really distinct from understanding of terms where the act is identical with power and object and infinite (God), or where the object is infinite and clearly understood (the blessed). Where the first object is finite, distinct acts are necessary.
claims: The blessed's theology is one simple act really, distinguished only by reason.
With an infinite object clearly known, one act can encompass terms, principles, and conclusions.
With a finite first object, distinct acts are necessary.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e1962.summary: The same holds of possible evident abstractive theology for wayfarers, whose first object is the divine essence evidently known though not seen. If, as someone might say, one act is needed only for the essence and simple terms, the answer would follow the note in the body of the question.
claims: Abstractive theology of wayfarers is similarly unified.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e1985.summary: To reconcile, one might say the essence is that by which all are known, but by several ordered acts, the prior a ratio of the posterior. Then one seeing the essence need not see all terms and necessary complexes, contrary to what was said. So the author holds with Augustine (De trinitate XV.14) that all our knowledge in the Word will be one act, really undistinct but distinct by reason. The blessed have no other abstractive theology, not because it is incompossible with vision but because it is unnecessary: when the perfect comes, the imperfect is done away (1 Cor 13).
claims: All the blessed's knowledge in the Word is one real act.
The blessed do not need abstractive theology, since the perfect supersedes the imperfect.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e2037.summary: Objection: the blessed have other sciences of things in their own genus (geometry, arithmetic), so why not an abstractive theology beside their vision? Reply: possible absolutely but neither fitting nor necessary. Theology has God as first object, so it is most fully had in its own genus when had in God seen; there is no distinction between visual theology in the Word and theology in its own genus, though vision and abstraction are distinct. All their knowledge of things in the Word belongs to their theology, so other sciences of things in their own genus are fitting, but no other theology.
claims: The blessed have other sciences of things in their own genus but need no other theology.
Theology in the Word is theology in its own genus most fully.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e2098.summary: Hence the blessed's theology is distinct from all others: from God's theology, from any possible abstractive theology (being intuitive), from ours, from any naturally had science, and from their other sciences in their own genus, since its first object is God under deity, while theirs are the things they concern.
claims: The blessed's theology is distinct from every other science by its intuitive character and first object.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e2122.summary: On subalternation, the blessed's theology is subalternate to none: the only candidate would be God's theology, which subalternates none; and God's and the blessed's theology concern the same first subject and truths. The objection that it is subalternate to metaphysics, God falling under being, will be answered below.
claims: The blessed's theology is subalternate to no science.
Theologies with the same subject and first truths do not subalternate one another.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e2146.summary: It subalternates none: the likeliest candidate is our theology, but faith is not subalternate to science, only science to science. Also subalternating and subalternate sciences are essentially ordered as prior and posterior, but this theology is not of the same order as others, being visual while they are abstractive, and abstractive and intuitive are only accidentally ordered.
claims: Faith is not subalternate to science.
Intuitive and abstractive knowledges are only accidentally ordered and cannot subalternate.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e2177.summary: On possible evident abstractive theology for wayfarers, the author would say the same as for the blessed's visual theology regarding unity and distinctness.
claims: Possible abstractive theology is unified and distinct like the blessed's.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e2191.summary: Regarding subalternation, abstractive theology is subalternate to none for the same reason, and subalternates none, not even our theology, since they share the same first object and first truths, one evident and one not, and our theology is not and cannot become science properly.
claims: Possible abstractive theology neither subalternates nor is subalternated.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e2209.summary: On our theology as doctors have it, a preliminary: whether our understanding of its first object, God, is one simple indivisible act or an aggregated concept from many (by understanding or removing imperfections) will be treated in d3, as will the acquired habit of its principles or quasi-principles.
claims: Whether our concept of God is simple or aggregated is deferred to d3.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e2229.summary: From these principles it deduces conclusions. Our theology is not simply one and indivisible but multiplied according to distinct principles and complexes. One can be acquired without another by frequent consideration of one and not another, whether the principles are articles of faith or not, as with habits of principles in other sciences. This concerns the acquired habit; whether infused faith in the articles is multiplied will be treated in a reply below. These are several habits ordered like their first objects, the complexes posited as principles from which conclusions are deduced.
claims: Our acquired theology comprises many habits, distinguished by principles and conclusions.
Acquired habits are separable by frequency of consideration.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e2273.summary: Likewise our theology, as the habit of conclusions deduced from those principles, is not one habit of most specific species but many habits, or an aggregate of specifically distinct partial habits according to the distinct conclusions, with some order. These constitute one total habit including habits of conclusions, of principles, and knowledge of terms, among which knowledge of the subject, God, is simply first; relative to this total habit God was posited as subject. So our theology is one only by order, like geometry, and one can have the habit of one conclusion while ignoring another, at least a prior without a posterior.
claims: Our theology is an aggregate of specifically distinct habits unified by order.
God is subject of theology as object of its first simple knowledge.
One conclusion's habit can be had without another's.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e2330.summary: Hence they are not one undivided habit, else the same would be had without itself. Our theology is distinct from all others: it is inevident and they evident; no other human science has God under deity as subject; it alone concerns what is naturally known only to God; and all others can have their due certainty without faith, while it cannot.
claims: Our theology is distinct from all others by inevidence, subject, object, and dependence on faith.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e2359.summary: On subalternation, our theology is subalternate neither to God's, nor the blessed's, nor possible abstractive theology, nor to any human science, of which metaphysics is the likeliest. Though its subject falls under being, it adds nothing outside the ratio of being, since nothing escapes being (predicated quidditatively of all, on a common opinion the author doubts), whereas a subalternate subject adds to the higher one, as visual line to line. It does not take its principles from metaphysics to prove its chief conclusions such as the Trinity. And it cannot become evident by any addition, while metaphysics is evident.
claims: Our theology is subalternate to no science.
God adds nothing outside the ratio of being.
Theology's chief conclusions are not provable from metaphysical principles.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e2417.summary: Summary: thus it is clear how theology is one habit, distinct from others, and how it subalternates or is subalternated. Ends the third article and begins the fourth.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e2430.summary: Fourth article, replies. To the first opinion's first argument: theology as a total aggregate need not be one simple habit though its first object, God, is one under one ratio; God is first object of the whole because he is the object of the first theological knowledge, the simple apprehension of the subject. Unity of subject does not suffice, and the total theology contains many habits each with its own adequate first object, so they are diversified by primary objects, not secondary ones.
claims: Theology's unity of first object does not make it one simple habit.
Its component habits are diversified by their own primary objects.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e2469.summary: To the confirmation about faith: whatever holds of infused faith, an acquired habit must be diversified by objects, since it can be had of one object and not another and depends on distinct acts about distinct objects; neither holds of infused faith.
claims: Acquired habits are diversified by objects; infused faith may not be.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e2495.summary: To the argument from essential order: theology need be one only by order and nobler than others, like geometry or astronomy. Simple unity among the first habits is impossible for wayfarers' sciences; it exists only in divine science and the blessed's science in the Word. All cognitive habits reduce to that supremely one divine science, as all beings to God.
claims: Simple unity belongs only to divine and beatific science.
All cognitive habits reduce to divine science as their first.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e2528.summary: To the third: granted that wayfarers' theology arises immediately from divine science, it need not be one simple habit; the unity found in other sciences plus excellence in nobility of object suffices.
claims: Theology's derivation from divine science does not make it simply one.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e2544.summary: The opposite opinion's reasons are granted insofar as they show theology is not one simple habit, but they conclude too much: that theology of eternal necessary things and of doable or contingent things are no more one than geometry and arithmetic, which is false.
claims: Speculative and practical theology are more unified than geometry and arithmetic.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e2574.summary: Reply to its first argument: theology treats actions by order and attribution to its first subject, God under deity, and need not treat them in sciences as distinct as Aristotle's metaphysics and ethics. Regarding the end, theological and philosophical morals share the same ultimate extrinsic end, God, though the theological immediate end, supernatural formal beatitude, attains God more perfectly. That does not make them distinct sciences, since metaphysics does not treat the final end of action as its subject while theology of necessary things does. So moral theology reduces to speculative theology and they are more one than metaphysics and ethics. Yet the theologian treats actions no less perfectly than the philosopher. On the opponents' view theology would be less one than ethics and metaphysics, since they say ethics is ordered to metaphysics as operation to contemplative happiness. Theologians treat actions not for speculation's sake.
claims: Moral theology treats action by attribution to God and is not a distinct science from speculative theology.
Theological and philosophical ethics share the same ultimate end, God, but differ in immediate end.
Theology treats actions as perfectly as philosophy, without needing a separate science.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e2676.summary: Reply to the second: because all beings agree in being, it cannot be said that metaphysics contains all science of every being, since being is not one real thing to which they reduce by a real relation. But everything treated in theology reduces to its first object as to something most truly one, to which they have a real relation and which virtually contains them all. Beings agree more in being by predication, but more in God by virtual containment and reduction.
claims: Being unites beings by predication only; God unites them by virtual containment and real relation.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e2709.summary: Reply to the third: Aristotle could not make metaphysics and ethics one science as theology is one, since he did not treat the final end of action (God) or even the formal end (happiness) as first subject, but rather being. The theologian treats God under deity, end of all action, and is moved by this ratio throughout, so he can have one theology of morals and eternal things, one in the way geometry is one. The paragraph's last words introduce the next replies.
claims: Theology unites morals and eternals because its subject is the end of all action.
Aristotle's metaphysics did not take the end of action as subject.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e2744.summary: Heading: replies to the arguments that theology subalternates all others.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e2751.summary: Reply to the first: the principles of other sciences are not resolved or reduced to theology, which is simply less evident than all others. Though it considers all things in a way as effects of a cause, it does not do so evidently.
claims: Theology's consideration of all as effects of God is not evident and grounds no subalternation.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e2769.summary: Reply to the second: theology does not subalternate practical sciences, though it prescribes their end, because it does not evidently show that this end, as beatific object or act, is their end, as the architectonic end is evidently the manual art's end by the nature of things.
claims: Prescribing an end non-evidently does not subalternate.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e2788.summary: The arguments that theology is subalternate to none are granted in conclusion, but one premise fails, namely that it subalternates all others, so that reasoning is invalid. The others are more probable and are left in peace.
claims: Theology is subalternate to none, though not because it subalternates all.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e2804.summary: Reply to the first principal argument: from the primacy and nobility of our theology it does not follow that it is one simple habit, which is impossible. Divine theology is maximally one, being most perfect and simply first, but ours is one only in the genus of our sciences, none of which is simply one habit.
claims: Only divine theology is maximally one; ours is one only as our sciences are.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e2830.summary: Reply to the second: God is subject of part of metaphysics, but that part with others constitutes one total science with being as adequate subject, while our theology has God as first and adequate subject; so no total human science has the same subject under the same ratio. Metaphysics treats God not as adequate subject but as cause of the parts of its subject, always by reduction to being. Unity of first object alone does not suffice for unity of science.
claims: Metaphysics treats God as cause of parts of its subject, not as adequate subject.
No human science shares theology's adequate subject under the same ratio.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e2869.summary: Reply to the third: though the theologian has the same concepts of terms as others, he forms other conclusions or complexes or deduces them differently, so has another science; formal science is not a heap of species of simple terms.
claims: Sharing concepts of terms does not make sciences identical.
Science is not a heap of species of terms.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e2891.summary: Reply to the fourth: containment of subject under subject does not suffice for subalternation.
claims: Containment of subjects is insufficient for subalternation.

qrdBas-a14289-d1e2898.summary: Reply to the fifth: though theology sometimes takes immediate truths declared in other sciences, it can never, as theology, reduce them evidently to self-evident truths, or to metaphysics or any other science as prior. The remaining two arguments for theology subalternating others were answered above.
claims: Theology's borrowing from other sciences does not make it subalternate.

qrdBas-a14289.summary: Prologue q6 asks four things: whether theology is one undivided habit, whether it is distinct from all naturally acquirable sciences, whether it subalternates any, and whether it is subalternate to any. Bassolis reports opinions on each member: theology is simply one (by unity of subject, a single primary object, essential order of habits) versus simply many (speculative and practical theology as distinct as metaphysics and ethics). He also reports grounds for distinctness (subject, principles, inevidence, faith) and claims that theology subalternates all sciences (by giving the propter quid of their principles, prescribing their end), against claims that it subalternates none. In the second article he analyses the unity of a science. Formal science is the habit of a conclusion, distinct conclusions have distinct habits (one can be had without another), and geometry or theology is one only by order as a 'total science'. Specific unity requires unity of conclusion, subject, and middle (as with propter quid versus quia, or proofs through different causes), but not unity of the receiving subject, since charity is the same in angels and men. Whether unity of light is required he leaves in doubt, inclining to think light only manifests. Applying this, God's theology is one infinite act, distinguished only by reason into simple understanding, understanding of principles, and science; it neither subalternates nor is subalternated, since other sciences have their own evidence and clarity is not subalternation. The blessed's theology is one act in the Word, needing no further abstractive theology. Our theology is an aggregate of specifically distinct habits, one by order, distinct from all others (inevident, about God under deity, dependent on faith), and subalternate to none, not even metaphysics, since God adds nothing outside being and theology does not take its chief principles from metaphysics. Moral and speculative theology form one science by attribution to God as end of all action, more unified than Aristotle's ethics and metaphysics.
claims: Formal science is the habit of a single conclusion; a 'science' like geometry or our theology is one only by order.
Specific unity of science requires unity of conclusion, subject, and middle, not of the receiving subject; unity of light is doubtful.
God's and the blessed's theology are each one act, distinguished only by reason.
Our theology is an aggregate of distinct habits, distinct from all other sciences, and neither subalternating nor subalternate to any.
Moral and speculative theology form one science by attribution to God as end.
